title: Nyāya Sūtra

attribution.tradition: Composed by the sage Gautama (Gotama), called Akṣapāda.
attribution.scholarly: A layered text; the definitional core of book 1 may be older, while the polemical sections of books 2–4 engage Buddhist views (incl. positions later associated with Madhyamaka and Yogācāra); final redaction usually placed c. 2nd–3rd c. CE.

tradition.text: ancient; the sage Gautama (no fixed date in the tradition)

scholarly.text: c. 2nd–3rd c. CE for the extant redaction (earlier layers possible)

structure.description: 5 adhyāyas × 2 āhnikas; about 528–535 sūtras depending on the edition (DCS e-text: 535). Two numbering systems are current: the DCS / raw_etexts numbering (used for teaching ids in this unit) and that of the Taranatha edition printed with the Nyāyabhāṣya, which diverges from 2.1.20, 2.2.43, 3.1.15, 3.2.34 and 5.1.4 onward.

summary: The root text of Nyāya. It opens by promising the highest good (niḥśreyasa) from knowledge of the truth of sixteen categories (NS 1.1.1), states the chain from false knowledge to liberation (1.1.2), defines the four means of knowledge, the twelve objects of knowledge beginning with the self, the five-membered demonstration, debate, pseudo-reasons, quibbles, futile rejoinders and points of defeat (book 1); examines the means of knowledge (book 2), the self, body, senses, cognition and mind (book 3), faults, rebirth, fruit, pain, liberation, the whole and atoms, rival views such as momentariness and idealism, and the yogic means to knowledge of truth (book 4); and lists the twenty-four futile rejoinders and twenty-two points of defeat (book 5).

editions.licence: CC BY 4.0 (DCS data); the ancient text itself is public domain

Nyāyadarśana with Vātsyāyana's Bhāṣya, ed. Taranatha Nyaya-Tarkatirtha and Amarendramohan Tarkatirtha (Calcutta Sanskrit Series 18, 1936)

title: Nyāyabhāṣya

attribution.tradition: Vātsyāyana, also called Pakṣilasvāmin (so named by Vācaspati).
attribution.scholarly: Vātsyāyana; before Dignāga, who criticizes him.

summary: Vātsyāyana's commentary, the oldest extant on the Nyāya Sūtra. It explains that a means of knowledge is purposeful because it makes action successful, defines nyāya as the examination of things by the means of knowledge, presents ānvīkṣikī as the fourth science distinct from the Upaniṣadic science of the self, reads the five members as a convergence of all four means of knowledge, catalogues the forms of false knowledge, rejects eternal pleasure in liberation, describes Īśvara as a distinct self who assists human effort, and prescribes yama, niyama, yoga and contemplation of the unlovely against passion.

editions.name: GRETIL/Sansknet e-text of the Nyāyabhāṣya (ed. Taranatha Nyaya-Tarkatirtha, Calcutta Sanskrit Series 18, 1936)

title: Nyāyavārttika

attribution.tradition: Uddyotakara Bhāradvāja; the colophon calls him a Pāśupata teacher.
attribution.scholarly: Uddyotakara, answering Dignāga; himself answered by Dharmakīrti's circle.

summary: Uddyotakara's sub-commentary defending the Nyāya Sūtra and Bhāṣya against Dignāga and other Buddhist critics ('bad reasoners'); it enumerates the six kinds of sense-object contact, defends the self, the whole, universals and Īśvara, and criticizes Buddhist definitions of perception and inference.
notes: Printed editions exist (e.g. Kashi Sanskrit Series); no local e-text was found in sources_raw.

title: Nyāyavārttikatātparyaṭīkā
summary: Vācaspati Miśra's gloss on the Nyāyavārttika. Its opening verses invoke Śiva (Pinākin) and Akṣapāda and state the aim of rescuing Uddyotakara's aged words sunk in the mire of bad commentaries; it answers Dharmakīrti's school, reads NS 1.1.4 as covering indeterminate and determinate perception, and names the twenty-one kinds of pain whose absolute cessation is the goal.

editions.name: GRETIL/Sansknet e-text (checked against the ed. of Anantalal Thakur, New Delhi 1996)

title: Nyāyasūcīnibandha

scholarly.text: 841 CE (if Vikrama era) or 976 CE (if Śaka era)

summary: Vācaspati Miśra's index of the sūtras and prakaraṇas of the Nyāya Sūtra, which fixed the sūtra text as read by the later tradition; its closing verse gives a date (year 898 of an unnamed era).

title: Nyāyavārttikatātparyapariśuddhi
summary: Udayana's sub-commentary on Vācaspati's Tātparyaṭīkā, continuing the defence of the Nyāya commentarial line.

title: Nyāyapariśiṣṭa
summary: Udayana's treatment of the fifth book of the Nyāya Sūtra (futile rejoinders and points of defeat); also known as Bodhasiddhi.
notes: Title and scope recalled, not checked.

title: Nyāyakusumāñjali

structure.description: 5 stabakas of kārikās with Udayana's prose; verse numbering varies by edition

summary: Udayana's 'handful of flowers of reasoning' offered to the Lord: in five clusters (stabaka) of verses with his own prose, it answers five objections to Īśvara — that there is no supersensible means to the other world, that such means can work without Him, that there are proofs of His non-existence, that even if He exists He is not an authority, and that there is no proof of Him — and gives, in 5.1, the classic list of proofs. It presents reasoning about the Lord as a form of worship and opens with a passage on the names under which the schools worship Him.
notes: Commentaries include Vardhamāna's Prakāśa; verse numbers used in this unit are from memory and marked low.

title: Ātmatattvaviveka
summary: Udayana's defence of an enduring self against Buddhist positions, organized as refutations of momentariness (kṣaṇabhaṅga), of the denial of external objects (bāhyārthabhaṅga), of the denial of the difference between quality and qualified (guṇaguṇibhedabhaṅga), and of the argument from the non-apprehension of a self (anupalambha); it closes with the knowledge of the self and liberation.
notes: Commented on by Raghunātha Śiromaṇi (Dīdhiti) and Mathurānātha. The alternative title is recalled, not checked.

title: Lakṣaṇāvalī

tradition.text: Śaka 906 = 984 CE (the text's own closing verse, as usually read)

scholarly.text: 984 CE is widely accepted; some scholars place Udayana later (11th c.)

summary: Udayana's short manual of definitions of the Vaiśeṣika categories, which divides the categories into positive ones (the six) and absence as a seventh; its closing verse dates it to Śaka 906 (984 CE).

title: Kiraṇāvalī (Udayana)
summary: Udayana's commentary on Praśastapāda's Padārthadharmasaṅgraha; it explains why absence is not listed among the categories there (because it is determined through its counterpositive, not because it is unreal) and gives the six impediments to a genuine universal (jātibādhaka).
notes: Sub-commentaries: Vardhamāna's Kiraṇāvalīprakāśa, Raghunātha's Dīdhiti on the Prakāśa.

title: Nyāyakusumāñjaliprakāśa
summary: Vardhamāna Upādhyāya's commentary on Udayana's Nyāyakusumāñjali.

title: Nyāyamañjarī
summary: Jayanta Bhaṭṭa's large independent exposition of Nyāya in twelve āhnikas, organized around the means of knowledge and the objects of knowledge; it defends the authority of the Veda and of the Lord, criticizes Buddhist, Mīmāṃsaka and Cārvāka positions, and discusses the validity of the Āgamas.

title: Nyāyakalikā
summary: A short manual of Nyāya attributed to Jayanta Bhaṭṭa.

title: Āgamaḍambara
summary: Jayanta Bhaṭṭa's philosophical drama in which representatives of rival religious and philosophical schools (Buddhist, Jain, Mīmāṃsaka, Śaiva and others, and the heterodox Nīlāmbaras) argue in Kashmir under King Śaṅkaravarman; the Naiyāyika position prevails.
notes: The alternative title is recalled with low confidence.

title: Nyāyasāra
summary: Bhāsarvajña's manual in three chapters (perception, inference, verbal testimony): it accepts only three means of knowledge, treats yogic perception, and holds — against the mainstream — that liberation is the absolute cessation of pain together with the experience of eternal bliss; its last part links the path to Śaiva yoga.

title: Nyāyabhūṣaṇa
summary: Bhāsarvajña's own extensive commentary on his Nyāyasāra, the main source for his independent positions (three means of knowledge; bliss in liberation).

title: Tārkikarakṣā
summary: Varadarāja's verse manual of Nyāya with auto-commentary, a standard pre-Gaṅgeśa handbook.

title: Tarkabhāṣā (Keśava Miśra)
summary: Keśava Miśra's primer of syncretic Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika, arranged by the sixteen categories of the Nyāya Sūtra and absorbing the Vaiśeṣika ontology into the treatment of the objects of knowledge; widely taught with many commentaries. (Distinct from Mokṣākaragupta's Buddhist Tarkabhāṣā.)

title: Tarkabhāṣāprakāśikā
summary: Cinnambhaṭṭa's commentary on Keśava Miśra's Tarkabhāṣā; it opens with a salutation to Maheśvara, 'whose breath is the Vedas'.
notes: Author and title as given by the local e-text header; date not checked.

title: Nyāyaratna
summary: Maṇikaṇṭha Miśra's pre-Gaṅgeśa work on inference and related topics, regarded as a forerunner of Navya-Nyāya.
notes: Low confidence on title details; listed as a gap to check.

title: Nyāyasiddhāntadīpa
summary: Śaśadhara's pre-Gaṅgeśa treatise on Nyāya topics.

title: Tattvacintāmaṇi

scholarly.text: first half of the 14th c. CE (Mithilā)

structure.description: 4 khaṇḍas: Pratyakṣa, Anumāna, Upamāna, Śabda; each divided into vādas

summary: Gaṅgeśa Upādhyāya's 'wish-gem of truth', the founding text of Navya-Nyāya, in four books (khaṇḍa) on perception, inference, comparison and verbal testimony. It treats validity as extrinsic, error as misplaced apprehension, sets out and rejects five provisional definitions of pervasion (vyāptipañcaka) before its own definition, defines subjecthood (pakṣatā) and consideration (parāmarśa), proves Īśvara by inference, and defines verbal testimony and the conditions of verbal cognition.

editions.name: GRETIL/Sansknet e-text of the Śabdakhaṇḍa (partial; Bibliotheca Indica ed.)

notes: The whole text survives in print; only the Śabdakhaṇḍa (partial) and the Vyāptipañcaka section were found digitized locally. Commentaries: Pakṣadhara's Āloka, Raghunātha's Dīdhiti, Mathurānātha's Rahasya, and many others.

title: Tattvacintāmaṇyāloka
summary: Pakṣadhara Miśra's (Jayadeva's) commentary on the Tattvacintāmaṇi, the principal Mithilā gloss before Raghunātha.

title: Tattvacintāmaṇidīdhiti
summary: Raghunātha Śiromaṇi's commentary on the Tattvacintāmaṇi, the foundation of the Navadvīpa school, itself the object of the great sub-commentaries of Jagadīśa (Jāgadīśī), Gadādhara (Gādādharī) and Bhavānanda.

title: Padārthatattvanirūpaṇa
summary: Raghunātha Śiromaṇi's critical re-examination of the Vaiśeṣika list of categories, proposing reductions and additions to the traditional seven.
notes: The specific revisions (e.g. treatment of space, time and ultimate particularity) are recalled with low confidence and are not asserted as teachings in this skeleton.

title: Ākhyātavāda (Raghunātha)
summary: Raghunātha Śiromaṇi's short treatise on the meaning of verbal endings (ākhyāta).

title: Nañvāda
summary: Raghunātha Śiromaṇi's treatise on the meaning of the negative particle (nañ).

title: Ātmatattvavivekadīdhiti
summary: Raghunātha Śiromaṇi's commentary on Udayana's Ātmatattvaviveka.

title: Tattvacintāmaṇirahasya
summary: Mathurānātha Tarkavāgīśa's commentary (the 'Māthurī') on the Tattvacintāmaṇi; he also wrote Rahasyas on the Dīdhiti and on Udayana's works.

title: Jāgadīśī
summary: Jagadīśa Tarkālaṅkāra's sub-commentary on Raghunātha's Dīdhiti.

title: Śabdaśaktiprakāśikā
summary: Jagadīśa Tarkālaṅkāra's verse treatise with auto-commentary on the semantics of words, case-endings, compounds and verbal cognition in Navya-Nyāya terms.

title: Tarkāmṛta
summary: Jagadīśa Tarkālaṅkāra's elementary manual of Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika.

title: Gādādharī
summary: Gadādhara Bhaṭṭācārya's voluminous sub-commentary on the Dīdhiti.

title: Vyutpattivāda
summary: Gadādhara Bhaṭṭācārya's treatise on how verbal cognition is produced from case-endings and word-meanings (the analysis of śābdabodha).

title: Śaktivāda
summary: Gadādhara Bhaṭṭācārya's treatise on the denotative power (śakti) of words and how it is grasped; commented on in the Mañjūṣā and Vinodinī.

title: Sāmānyanirukti (Gādādharī)
summary: Gadādhara's commentary on the section of the Tattvacintāmaṇi (with Dīdhiti) that gives the general definition of pseudo-reasons (hetvābhāsa-sāmānya-nirukti).

title: Muktivāda (Raghudeva)
summary: A Navya-Nyāya treatise on liberation that opens with the Ācārya's (Udayana's) definition of liberation as the absolute cessation of pain and refines 'absolute' in technical terms; one of a set of vāda texts attributed to Raghudeva Bhaṭṭācārya.
notes: Attribution follows the local e-text header; the same collection contains Īśvaravāda, Prāgabhāvavāda, Ākāṅkṣāvāda, Sāmagrīvāda and other vādas.

title: Bhāṣāpariccheda

scholarly.text: first half of the 17th c. CE

summary: Viśvanātha Nyāyapañcānana's verse compendium (kārikāvalī) of Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika, opening with a salutation to Kṛṣṇa as the seed of the tree of saṃsāra and listing seven categories; read with his own commentary, the Siddhāntamuktāvalī.

title: Nyāyasiddhāntamuktāvalī

scholarly.text: first half of the 17th c. CE

summary: Viśvanātha's auto-commentary on the Bhāṣāpariccheda, the standard intermediate text of syncretic Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika in Navya-Nyāya idiom (e.g. its inference of a maker from the effecthood of earth, sprouts and the like).

title: Dinakarī
summary: Dinakara Bhaṭṭa's commentary on the Nyāyasiddhāntamuktāvalī.
notes: Printed together with the Rāmarudrī in the local OCR e-text.

title: Rāmarudrī
summary: Rāmarudra Bhaṭṭa's commentary on the Nyāyasiddhāntamuktāvalī (a gloss continuing the Dinakarī).

title: Nyāyasūtravṛtti (Viśvanātha)

scholarly.text: 1634 CE (date given in the text, as usually reported)

summary: Viśvanātha Nyāyapañcānana's running commentary on the Nyāya Sūtra, in Navya-Nyāya idiom.

title: Tarkasaṅgraha
summary: Annambhaṭṭa's primer of syncretic Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika 'for the easy understanding of beginners': seven categories, nine substances, twenty-four qualities, five motions, two kinds of universal, endless particularities, one inherence and four absences; the self as the substrate of cognition (the one omniscient Lord and the many embodied selves); the four means of knowledge with the Navya definitions of pervasion, consideration, pseudo-reasons, the denotative power of words as the Lord's convention, and the conditions of verbal cognition.

editions.licence: CC BY 4.0 (DCS data); the ancient text itself is public domain

notes: Teaching refs for this prose manual are topic names, not section numbers (editions number sections differently).

title: Tarkasaṅgrahadīpikā
summary: Annambhaṭṭa's own commentary on the Tarkasaṅgraha, supplying arguments (e.g. for Īśvara) and Navya-Nyāya refinements.

title: Tarkakaumudī
summary: Laugākṣi Bhāskara's short manual of Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika.

title: Maṇikaṇa
summary: A short Navya-Nyāya manual (author uncertain), edited by E. R. Sreekrishna Sarma (Adyar Library, 1960).
notes: Known here only from the local e-text header; contents not examined.

title: Navyanyāyabhāṣāpradīpa
summary: Maheśacandra Nyāyaratna's brief guide to the technical language of Navya-Nyāya (with the Suprabhā commentary and a Bengali translation by Kālīpada Tarkācārya in the printed edition).

title: Vaiśeṣika Sūtra

attribution.tradition: Composed by the sage Kaṇāda (Kaṇabhuj, Ulūka, Kāśyapa).
attribution.scholarly: A layered text transmitted in divergent recensions; the recension commented on by Candrānanda is older than that of Śaṅkara Miśra's Upaskāra, which contains sūtras absent from it (e.g. Upaskāra 1.1.4 listing the six categories).

scholarly.text: core perhaps c. 1st c. BCE – 1st c. CE (estimates vary widely); extant recensions redacted later

structure.description: 10 adhyāyas; in Candrānanda's recension books 1–8 have two āhnikas (book 8 one) and books 9–10 none; c. 370–385 sūtras depending on recension. Teaching ids in this unit use Candrānanda's numbering (DCS e-text); Upaskāra numbers are noted where known.

summary: The root text of Vaiśeṣika in ten books. It announces the explanation of dharma — that from which prosperity and the highest good result — and grounds the Veda's authority; lists the nine substances, the qualities and the five motions and defines substance, quality and motion; treats being, universals and particulars, the elements, time, space, the self (with its marks and plurality) and the atomic mind; atoms and perception; motions caused by the unseen (adṛṣṭa); yoga and liberation; ethics of giving, food and ritual observances; inherence; absence; perception, inference and memory; and the seers' knowledge.

editions.licence: CC BY 4.0 (DCS data); the ancient text itself is public domain

editions.name: Vaiśeṣikasūtra of Kaṇāda with the commentary of Candrānanda, ed. Muni Jambuvijaya (Gaekwad's Oriental Series 136, 1961)

title: Vaiśeṣikasūtravṛtti (Candrānanda)

scholarly.text: uncertain; estimates range c. 7th–10th c. CE

summary: Candrānanda's brief commentary, the oldest complete commentary on the Vaiśeṣika Sūtra, transmitting the older recension of the sūtras.

editions.name: Digital Corpus of Sanskrit (DCS) e-text, github.com/OliverHellwig/sanskrit (Vaiśeṣikasūtravṛtti)
editions.licence: CC BY 4.0 (DCS data); the ancient text itself is public domain

title: Upaskāra
summary: Śaṅkara Miśra's commentary on the Vaiśeṣika Sūtra, for centuries the standard one; it transmits the later recension of the sūtras (with, e.g., the sūtra listing the six categories as 1.1.4) and reads the Veda's authority as grounded in its being the Lord's statement.

title: Vādivinoda
summary: Śaṅkara Miśra's work on the conduct of debate; later authors cite it for the statement that the followers of Kaṇāda and of Gautama accept seven categories.

title: Padārthadharmasaṅgraha
summary: Praśastapāda's systematic exposition of Vaiśeṣika (often called Praśastapādabhāṣya, though not a line-by-line commentary): after saluting Īśvara and Kaṇāda it declares knowledge of the similarities and dissimilarities of the six categories the cause of the highest good, arising from dharma manifested by the Lord's command; it fixes twenty-four qualities, gives the account of cosmic dissolution and creation by Maheśvara's will, divides cognition into knowledge (perception, inference, memory, seers' knowledge) and its opposites, treats yogic perception, dharma and adharma, and liberation.
notes: Commentaries: Vyomaśiva's Vyomavatī, Śrīdhara's Nyāyakandalī, Udayana's Kiraṇāvalī, and later ones.

title: Vyomavatī

scholarly.text: c. 10th c. CE (some place it earlier)

summary: Vyomaśiva's commentary on the Padārthadharmasaṅgraha, the oldest extant one.

title: Nyāyakandalī
summary: Śrīdhara's commentary on the Padārthadharmasaṅgraha, dated in its colophon to Śaka 913 (991 CE); it defends Īśvara and the Vaiśeṣika categories against Buddhist and Mīmāṃsaka critics.

title: Nyāyalīlāvatī
summary: Śrīvallabha's independent Vaiśeṣika treatise; later authors cite it for the view that absence must be stated as a category because it serves the highest good.

title: Saptapadārthī
summary: Śivāditya's compact manual that expounds the categories as seven — the six of Kaṇāda with absence — and blends Nyāya epistemology into Vaiśeṣika.

title: Daśapadārthaśāstra

scholarly.text: before 648 CE (date of the Chinese translation)

summary: Candramati's Vaiśeṣika treatise of ten categories — substance, quality, motion, universal, particularity, inherence, capacity (śakti), incapacity (aśakti), the universal-particular (sāmānyaviśeṣa) and absence — lost in Sanskrit and preserved only in Xuanzang's Chinese translation (648 CE).
notes: Taishō no. 2138 (from memory, to be checked); CBETA has the Chinese text.
